title: Calculus I: limits, derivatives and an introduction to the integral
summary: A first course in single-variable calculus for first-year undergraduates. Students learn limits and continuity, the derivative and its rules, and its applications to related rates, optimization and curve sketching. The course ends with the definite integral and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
brief: Calculus I for first-year undergraduates: a 15-week semester, three 50-minute lectures a week and one 50-minute recitation led by a teaching assistant. Limits and continuity, derivatives and their rules, applications of the derivative (related rates, optimization, curve sketching), and an introduction to the integral. Textbook: Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals. Weekly online homework 15%, weekly recitation quizzes 15%, two midterms 20% each, final exam 30%.

l_4e658ad6a9ac.summary: Motivates limits with tangent and velocity problems, then evaluates limits from graphs, tables and the limit laws; recitation quiz in the problem session.
readings: Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, ch. 2 (to confirm): the tangent and velocity problems, the limit of a function, calculating limits using the limit laws

segments.title: The course map and how it is assessed
segments.description:
Introduce yourself and the teaching assistant who leads the problem session. Name the textbook, Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals.
Walk through the grading: weekly online homework 15%, weekly recitation quizzes 15%, Midterm 1 20%, Midterm 2 20%, final exam 30%.
Explain that homework is each student’s own work, submitted online before the lesson it is due at, and that the recitation quiz is taken in the problem session.
Give the arc of the course: limits and continuity, derivatives and their rules, applications of the derivative, then the integral.
segments.teacherNotes: Nothing today rests on earlier reading. Say that chapter 2 of Stewart (the tangent and velocity problems, the limit of a function, the limit laws) is the book’s version of this week’s material. Readings are announced in each close from now on.

segments.title: The tangent problem
segments.description:
Pose the problem: find the line tangent to y = x² at P(1, 1). Point out that the slope formula needs two points and we have only one.
Choose a second point Q(x, x²) on the curve and write the slope of the secant line PQ.
Everyone writes one sentence on what should happen to Q so that the secant line becomes the tangent line, then two students read theirs.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: Q slides along the parabola toward P, so the secant pivots toward the tangent. Draw the parabola large with two or three secants. Students often think a tangent touches the curve only once; that fails for other curves, so stress slope.
shown: Find the line tangent to y = x² at P(1, 1).
Secant through P(1, 1) and Q(x, x²): m_PQ = (x² − 1)/(x − 1), for x ≠ 1

segments.title: Secant slopes closing in on P
segments.description:
In pairs, one partner computes m_PQ at x = 1.1 and x = 1.01, and the other computes m_PQ at x = 0.99.
Partners compare their three values and write one prediction for the slope of the tangent at P.
Hear one prediction and the reason given.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: x = 1.1: 2.1; 1.01: 2.01; 0.99: 1.99. Prediction: 2. Common slip: using x + 1 in the denominator, or forgetting the denominator. Calculators are fine. Cutting to three values keeps both sides of P.
shown: x = 1.1, 1.01 (Q to the right of P)
x = 0.99 (Q to the left of P)

segments.title: From secant slopes to a limit
segments.description:
For x ≠ 1, simplify (x² − 1)/(x − 1) to x + 1. Show that as x gets close to 1 but is never equal to 1, the slope gets close to 2.
Name this as the limit of the secant slopes and write the tangent line y − 1 = 2(x − 1), that is y = 2x − 1.
Point out that x = 1 itself gives 0/0, so the limit is a way to talk about values near 1 without using 1.
segments.teacherNotes: Do not formalize yet. Ask one student why the simplification is allowed only for x ≠ 1: the cancelled factor x − 1 is zero at x = 1.

segments.title: The velocity problem
segments.description:
Suppose a ball is dropped from a very tall tower (a hypothetical tower). After t seconds it has fallen s(t) = 4.9t² meters. Find its average velocity over [5, 6] as change in distance over change in time.
Everyone writes the number that best describes its speed at exactly t = 5.
Students work alone, then check with a neighbor, computing the average velocity over [5, 5.1], [5, 5.01] and [5, 5.001].
Each writes the number the averages approach and calls it the instantaneous velocity at t = 5.
segments.teacherNotes: Average on [5, 6]: (176.4 − 122.5)/1 = 53.9 m/s. Guesses vary from 49 to 54. Then 49.49, 49.049, 49.0049 m/s, approaching 49 m/s. Check: average on [5, 5 + h] is 49 + 4.9h. 4.9t² comes from g ≈ 9.8 m/s².
shown: Average velocity on [a, b] = (s(b) − s(a))/(b − a)

segments.title: What the two problems share
segments.description:
Students write for three minutes: what is the same in the tangent problem and the velocity problem?
Hear two or three answers and put the shared structure on the board: a ratio of change in output to change in input, over an interval that shrinks toward zero.
segments.teacherNotes: Target: both are limits of a difference quotient, and both give 0/0 if the interval width is set to 0. Accept any wording that names the ratio and the shrinking interval. This is why limits come first in the course.
shown: What is the same in the tangent problem and the velocity problem?

segments.title: Where we are going
segments.description:
Recap: a tangent slope and an instantaneous velocity each came out as a number that secant slopes or average velocities approach.
Tell students the next lecture gives this idea a name, the limit of a function, and estimates limits from tables and graphs.
Remind them the weekly recitation quiz is taken in the problem session.
segments.teacherNotes: Keep this brief. Students may look at the chapter 2 section on the limit of a function in Stewart before the next lecture.

segments.title: The limit of a function: an informal definition
segments.description:
State it: lim (x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) can be made as close to L as we like by taking x close enough to a, with x ≠ a.
Show the table for f(x) = x² − x + 2 near x = 2, from both sides.
Everyone writes the number f(x) seems to approach and the notation for it, then two students share.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: lim (x→2) (x² − x + 2) = 4. Here f(2) = 4 too, which the next example breaks. Stress that x ≠ a is part of the definition. Have students say aloud ‘from the left’ and ‘from the right’ for the two halves of the table.
shown: f(x) = x² − x + 2. Values of f(x) as x approaches 2:

segments.title: A table for sin x / x
segments.description:
With calculators in radian mode, one partner computes sin x / x for x = 0.5 and 0.1, and the other for x = −0.1.
Partners compare their three values, then write an estimate of lim (x→0) sin x / x.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: 0.9589 at 0.5 and 0.9983 at 0.1 and at −0.1, equal by symmetry; estimate 1. Frequent error: degree mode gives about 0.0175 for x = 0.5. If asked, note the function is undefined at 0 because the denominator is 0. Algebra cannot settle this limit yet; a graph supports it.

segments.title: The limit is not the value
segments.description:
Sketch g(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2), a line with a hole at (2, 4), and the function k with a point displaced at x = 2.
Everyone writes the limit as x → 2 and the value at 2 for each, before anyone answers.
Conclude that a limit can exist when the function is undefined, or defined with a different value, at that point.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: for g, limit 4 and g(2) undefined; for k, limit 4 and k(2) = 1. Misconception: ‘the limit is what the function equals at a.’ Contrast with the earlier table where limit and value happened to agree.
shown: k(x) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2, and k(2) = 1

segments.title: Reading limits from a graph
segments.description:
Introduce x→a⁻ as approaching a from the left and x→a⁺ as approaching a from the right. Show the function h by its pieces and have students picture its graph from the description.
Students answer the six questions alone for four minutes, then compare with a partner.
Go over each one, using a sketch of h.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: (a) 3; (b) 2; (c) does not exist; (d) h(0) = 1; (e) 2; (f) h(2) = 0. Students often answer (c) with 1 by reading the dot at x = 0. For (e), the value h(2) = 0 does not matter; near 2, h(x) = 2.

segments.title: One-sided limits and when a limit does not exist
segments.description:
Introduce lim (x→a⁻) and lim (x→a⁺), and the rule: lim (x→a) f(x) = L exactly when both one-sided limits equal L.
Apply it to f(x) = x + 1 for x < 2 and f(x) = x² for x ≥ 2, and to |x|/x at 0.
Students first write both one-sided limits for each function, then hear them.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: f: left 3, right 4, so the limit does not exist even though f(2) = 4. |x|/x: left −1, right 1, does not exist. Unbounded behavior is treated later in the course.
shown: f(x) = x + 1 for x < 2; f(x) = x² for x ≥ 2

segments.title: When a table misleads
segments.description:
Show the values of sin(π/x) at x = 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5. Everyone writes a prediction for the limit as x → 0.
Then show x = 2/5, 2/9, 2/13 and let students recompute.
Discuss what the two tables together say about relying on a table alone.
segments.teacherNotes: First table: every value is 0, so students predict 0. Then sin(π/x) = 1 at x = 2/5, 2/9, 2/13, since π/x = 5π/2, 9π/2, 13π/2. For positive integers n, x = 1/n gives value 0 and x = 2/(4n + 1) gives value 1. Both sequences approach 0, so the function does not approach a single value and the limit does not exist. Tables suggest; they do not prove.

segments.title: Estimating a limit
segments.description:
Recap the tools: tables, graphs, one-sided limits and the warning from sin(π/x).
Preview the next lecture, which evaluates limits by algebra with the limit laws.
segments.teacherNotes: If time remains, ask for one limit students could not settle from a table alone.

segments.title: The limit laws and direct substitution
segments.description:
State the laws for lim f = L and lim g = M: sum, difference, constant multiple, product, quotient (when M ≠ 0) and power.
Conclude that polynomials and rational functions can be evaluated by direct substitution when the denominator is not 0 at a.
Students first evaluate (a) alone, then compare with a neighbor.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer to (a): numerator −8 + 8 − 1 = −1, denominator 5 + 6 = 11, so −1/11. Each law needs the individual limits to exist. The quotient law’s condition M ≠ 0 is tested in the next examples.
shown: Suppose lim (x→a) f(x) = L and lim (x→a) g(x) = M. Then:

segments.title: Zero over zero: factor and cancel
segments.description:
Students try (b), (c) and (d) alone. For each, they factor or expand, cancel the common factor and write the limit.
One student shows (c) at the board.
segments.teacherNotes: Each item gives 0/0 under substitution; students need not write that out. (b) lim (x→3) (x² − x − 6)/(x − 3) = 5. (c) lim (x→1) (x² − 1)/(x² − 3x + 2) = −2, since the quotient simplifies to (x + 1)/(x − 2). (d) lim (h→0) ((3 + h)² − 9)/h = 6. Common slip in (d): not expanding (3 + h)².

segments.title: Square roots: multiply by the conjugate
segments.description:
Pose lim (h→0) (√(9 + h) − 3)/h. Students try to simplify for one minute and see what is stuck.
Multiply top and bottom by √(9 + h) + 3, cancel h and substitute.
Students write the limit and say to a partner why the cancellation is legitimate.
segments.teacherNotes: The numerator becomes (9 + h) − 9 = h, giving 1/(√(9 + h) + 3), whose limit is 1/6. Cancelling h is allowed because h ≠ 0 in a limit. Students may try to rationalize the denominator; steer them to the numerator.

segments.title: Find the mistake
segments.description:
Students receive three flawed solutions. For each they name the error, then write a correct solution.
They work alone for eight minutes, then compare with a partner.
Go over each, naming the rule that was misused.
segments.teacherNotes: A: correct is that 0/0 signals rewriting; the limit is 4. B: the expression equals 0 for x ≠ 0, so the limit is 0; the difference law needs both limits to exist. C: left limit 3, right limit 4, so the limit does not exist; f(2) is irrelevant.

segments.title: Choose the method
segments.description:
For each of three limits, students write the technique to use in one word: substitute, factor, or conjugate.
They then find the value of (i) and (ii), and for (iii) write the expression left after multiplying by the conjugate and cancelling.
Check on the board.
segments.teacherNotes: (i) lim (x→4) (x² − x)/(x + 1): substitute, 12/5. (ii) lim (x→2) (x² − 5x + 6)/(x − 2): factor, x − 3 gives −1. (iii) lim (x→0) (√(x + 4) − 2)/x: conjugate, 1/(√(x + 4) + 2); say aloud that its limit is 1/4.

segments.title: What the limit laws give us
segments.description:
Recap the decision: substitute when the denominator is not 0, rewrite when you get 0/0, and check the one-sided limits when a function changes formula.
Tell students the problem session works problems on all three lectures, then holds the weekly recitation quiz.
segments.teacherNotes: Suggest students bring questions on the ‘find the mistake’ items to the problem session.

segments.title: Problems on tangents, velocities and limits
segments.description:
The teaching assistant sets seven problems and students work in pairs, trying each before any solution is shown.
Problems 1 to 3 cover two secant slopes with a tangent estimate, the tangent line and a velocity limit. Problem 4 pairs a table estimate with algebra. Problem 5 asks for a limit found by expanding and cancelling.
Problems 6 and 7 use one-sided limits, the last one turned around: find the constant that makes a limit exist.

segments.title: Worked solutions
segments.description:
The teaching assistant works the seven problems at the board, naming the rule each step uses.
Students mark where their own work differed and ask about it.
Clear the board and the screen of all solutions before the quiz.
segments.teacherNotes: For 1, show (1/x − 1/2)/(x − 2) = −1/(2x), valid for x ≠ 2. For 4, stress that algebra confirms the table’s estimate. Contrast this with the misleading table for sin(π/x). Erase everything before the quiz.

keyIdeas: The slope of a tangent line and the instantaneous velocity of a moving object are both limits of average rates of change over shorter and shorter intervals.
The limit of f(x) as x approaches a describes what f(x) does near a, not at a. The value f(a) may differ from the limit, or may not exist.
Tables and graphs give estimates of limits. A table can mislead, as sin(π/x) near 0 shows, so estimates need a graph or algebra to back them.
The limit laws and direct substitution evaluate many limits. When substitution gives 0/0, rewrite the expression by factoring, expanding or multiplying by a conjugate.
A limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and are equal. When they differ, the limit does not exist.

vocabulary.definition: A line through two points on a curve. Its slope is the average rate of change between those points.
The line through a point on a curve whose slope is the limit of the secant slopes as the second point approaches it.
The number the average velocities approach as the time interval shrinks toward zero.
The value L that f(x) approaches as x approaches a, written lim (x→a) f(x) = L. It ignores the value at x = a.
The value f(x) approaches as x approaches a from the left (x→a⁻) or from the right (x→a⁺).
A limit does not exist when the one-sided limits differ or when f(x) does not settle on one number, as with sin(π/x) near 0.
Evaluating a limit by putting x = a into the formula, valid for polynomials and for rational functions whose denominator is not 0 at a.
For √A − B, the expression √A + B. Multiplying by it removes a square root from a numerator.

study.overview: This lesson shows that two problems that look different, finding a tangent line and finding an instantaneous velocity, both come down to one idea: the limit of a function. You then learn to estimate limits from tables and graphs, and to evaluate them with the limit laws. Along the way you meet one-sided limits, which decide when a limit does not exist. Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, chapter 2 (to confirm), covers the same material if you want a second explanation.

points.heading: Tangent slopes and instantaneous velocity are limits
points.explanation:
Both problems have the same obstacle: you want a rate of change at one instant or one point, but a rate needs two points. The fix is to compute an average rate over a short interval and let the interval shrink.

Tangent example. Find the tangent line to y = x² at P(1, 1). Take Q(x, x²) on the curve. The secant slope is m_PQ = (x² − 1)/(x − 1). For x ≠ 1 this simplifies to x + 1. At x = 1.1 the slope is 2.1, at x = 1.01 it is 2.01, and at x = 0.99 it is 1.99. The slopes approach 2 from both sides, so the tangent slope is 2 and the tangent line is y − 1 = 2(x − 1), that is y = 2x − 1. Putting x = 1 straight into the formula gives 0/0, so the limit lets us talk about values near 1 without using 1.

Velocity example. Suppose a ball is dropped from a hypothetical tall tower and has fallen s(t) = 4.9t² meters after t seconds. The average velocity on [5, 5 + h] is (s(5 + h) − s(5))/h = (49h + 4.9h²)/h = 49 + 4.9h for h ≠ 0. As h shrinks, this approaches 49 m/s, the instantaneous velocity at t = 5.

The shared structure is a ratio of change in output to change in input, over an interval that shrinks toward zero.

points.heading: A limit describes behavior near a, not at a
points.explanation:
The statement lim (x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) can be made as close to L as we like by taking x close enough to a, with x ≠ a. The value f(a) plays no role. It may equal the limit, differ from it, or not exist.

Example 1. Let g(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2). For x ≠ 2 this equals x + 2, so the graph is a line with a hole at (2, 4). The limit as x → 2 is 4, but g(2) is undefined.

Example 2. Let k(x) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2 and k(2) = 1. Near 2 the function behaves exactly like g, so the limit is 4, yet k(2) = 1.

One-sided limits make this precise. The notation x→a⁻ means approaching from the left, and x→a⁺ means approaching from the right. The limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and are equal.

Example 3. Let f(x) = x + 1 for x < 2 and f(x) = x² for x ≥ 2. The left limit at 2 is 3 and the right limit is 4. They differ, so lim (x→2) f(x) does not exist, even though f(2) = 4.

Example 4. For |x|/x at 0, the left limit is −1 and the right limit is 1. Again the limit does not exist.

points.heading: Tables and graphs estimate limits, but a table can mislead
points.explanation:
To estimate a limit from a table, choose x-values on both sides of a, close to a, and see whether f(x) settles toward one number.

Good example. With your calculator in radian mode, sin x / x is about 0.9589 at x = 0.5 and about 0.9983 at both x = 0.1 and x = −0.1. These values are equal by symmetry. The estimate is lim (x→0) sin x / x = 1, even though the function is undefined at 0. A graph supports the estimate. If your calculator is in degree mode, you will get about 0.0175 at x = 0.5, which is a sign of the wrong mode.

Misleading example. Look at sin(π/x) as x → 0. At x = 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 every value is 0, which suggests a limit of 0. But at x = 2/5, 2/9, 2/13 we have π/x = 5π/2, 9π/2, 13π/2, and the value is 1 each time. Both lists of x-values approach 0, yet the function values approach different numbers. So the function does not approach a single value, and the limit does not exist.

A table suggests an answer; it does not prove one. Back an estimate with a graph or with algebra.

points.heading: Limit laws, direct substitution and the zero-over-zero toolkit
points.explanation:
Suppose lim f(x) = L and lim g(x) = M as x → a. Then the limit of a sum, difference, constant multiple or product is the sum, difference, constant multiple or product of the limits. The limit of a quotient is L/M if M ≠ 0. The limit of [f(x)]ⁿ is Lⁿ. Each law needs the individual limits to exist.

So for polynomials, and for rational functions whose denominator is not 0 at a, you can substitute. Example: lim (x→−2) (x³ + 2x² − 1)/(5 − 3x). The numerator gives −8 + 8 − 1 = −1 and the denominator gives 5 + 6 = 11, so the limit is −1/11.

If substitution gives 0/0, the expression must be rewritten. 0/0 does not equal 0, and it does not mean the limit fails to exist. It means more work is needed.

Factor and cancel. For lim (x→3) (x² − x − 6)/(x − 3), write x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2). For x ≠ 3 the quotient is x + 2, so the limit is 5.

Conjugate. For lim (h→0) (√(9 + h) − 3)/h, multiply top and bottom by √(9 + h) + 3. The numerator becomes (9 + h) − 9 = h, and the quotient becomes 1/(√(9 + h) + 3) for h ≠ 0. Its limit is 1/6. Keep the +3 in the denominator when you multiply.

Cancelling is legitimate because in a limit x ≠ a, so the cancelled factor is not zero. Choose the method before you start: substitute if the denominator is not 0, rewrite if you get 0/0, and check both one-sided limits if the formula changes at a.

(b) 2. For positive x near 0, h(x) = 2.

handouts.title: Zero over zero: factor and cancel
handouts.usedIn: Zero over zero: factor and cancel

blocks.text: For each limit, factor or expand, cancel the common factor, and write the limit. Show your steps.

handouts.key:
(b) x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2). For x ≠ 3, (x² − x − 6)/(x − 3) = x + 2. Therefore, the limit is 3 + 2 = 5.
(c) x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1), and x² − 3x + 2 = (x − 1)(x − 2). For x ≠ 1 near 1, the quotient equals (x + 1)/(x − 2). Therefore, the limit is 2/(−1) = −2.
(d) (3 + h)² − 9 = 6h + h² = h(6 + h). For h ≠ 0, the quotient equals 6 + h. Therefore, the limit is 6.

handouts.title: Find the mistake

blocks.text: Each solution below contains an error. For each one, name the error, then write a correct solution.
Solution A
Find lim (x→2) (x² − 4)/(x − 2). Substitute x = 2. The result is 0/0, which equals 0. So the limit is 0.
Solution B
Find lim (x→0) (1/x − 1/x). By the difference law this equals lim (x→0) 1/x − lim (x→0) 1/x. Neither of these limits exists, so the limit of the difference does not exist.
Solution C
Let f(x) = x + 1 for x < 2 and f(x) = x² for x ≥ 2. Find lim (x→2) f(x). Since f(2) = 2² = 4, the limit is 4.

handouts.key:
Solution A — The error: 0/0 is undefined, not 0. Direct substitution does not determine this limit.
A correct solution: x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2). For x ≠ 2, (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = x + 2. Thus, lim (x→2) (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = 4.

Solution B — The error: the difference law requires both individual limits to exist as finite numbers. It cannot be applied to these two terms separately.
A correct solution: for every x ≠ 0, 1/x − 1/x = 0. Thus, lim (x→0) (1/x − 1/x) = 0. Look for simplification of the whole expression before taking its limit. Common slip: concluding that a difference has no limit because its separate terms have no limits.

Solution C — The error: f(2) does not determine the limit as x approaches 2.
A correct solution: lim (x→2⁻) f(x) = 2 + 1 = 3, while lim (x→2⁺) f(x) = 2² = 4. Since the one-sided limits differ, lim (x→2) f(x) does not exist. Look for both one-sided limits and a conclusion based on their disagreement.

handouts.title: Choose the method

blocks.text: For each limit, write the technique in one word: substitute, factor, or conjugate. Then find the value of (i) and (ii). For (iii), write the expression left after you multiply by the conjugate and cancel.

handouts.key:
(i) Technique: substitute. Value: (4² − 4)/(4 + 1) = 12/5.
(ii) Technique: factor. Since x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3), the quotient equals x − 3 for x ≠ 2. Value: −1.
(iii) Technique: conjugate. Multiplying numerator and denominator by √(x + 4) + 2 gives x/[x(√(x + 4) + 2)]. After canceling x for x ≠ 0, the expression is 1/(√(x + 4) + 2).
Common slips: treating 0/0 as the answer in (ii) or (iii), or failing to multiply both numerator and denominator by the conjugate.

handouts.title: Problems on tangents, velocities and limits

blocks.text: Work in pairs. Try each problem before any solution is shown. Calculators are fine.

blocks.label: Problem 1
blocks.value: Let P(2, 1/2) be a point on the curve y = 1/x. For Q(x, 1/x), find the slope of the secant line PQ for x = 3 and for x = 2.1 (give the second to four decimal places). Estimate the slope of the tangent line at P.

blocks.hint: Two secant slopes and your estimate

blocks.label: Problem 2
blocks.value: Use your estimate from Problem 1 to write the equation of the tangent line to y = 1/x at P(2, 1/2) in the form y = mx + b.

blocks.label: Problem 3
blocks.value: Suppose a ball is dropped from a hypothetical tower. After t seconds it has fallen s(t) = 4.9t² meters. For h ≠ 0, find and simplify the average velocity over [2, 2 + h]. Then find the instantaneous velocity at t = 2.

blocks.hint: Simplified average velocity and the limit, with units

blocks.label: Problem 4
blocks.value: Let f(x) = (√(x + 4) − 2)/x. Compute f(0.1) and f(−0.1) to four decimal places and estimate lim (x→0) f(x). Then find the limit algebraically.

blocks.hint: Two values, your estimate, and the algebra

blocks.label: Problem 6
blocks.value: Find the one-sided limits of |x − 3|/(x − 3) as x → 3⁻ and as x → 3⁺. Does lim (x→3) |x − 3|/(x − 3) exist?

blocks.hint: Both one-sided limits and your conclusion

blocks.label: Problem 7
blocks.value: Let f(x) = 2cx + 1 for x < 1 and f(x) = x + 2 for x ≥ 1, where c is a constant. Find the value of c for which lim (x→1) f(x) exists.

handouts.key:
Problem 1: m_PQ = (1/x − 1/2)/(x − 2) = [(2 − x)/(2x)]/(x − 2) = −1/(2x), for x ≠ 2. At x = 3, the slope is −1/6. At x = 2.1, the slope is −1/4.2 ≈ −0.2381. Estimated tangent slope: −1/4. Look for a negative slope approaching −0.25. Common slip: reversing the order of subtraction in only the numerator or denominator.

Problem 2: y − 1/2 = (−1/4)(x − 2), so y = −x/4 + 1. Common slip: using 1/2 as the y-intercept instead of using the point to find the intercept.

Problem 3: Average velocity = [4.9(2 + h)² − 4.9(2)²]/h = (19.6h + 4.9h²)/h = 19.6 + 4.9h m/s, for h ≠ 0. Its limit as h → 0 is 19.6 m/s, the instantaneous velocity at t = 2. Look for the difference quotient, its simplification, and units. Common slip: omitting the cross term when expanding (2 + h)².

Problem 4: f(0.1) = (√4.1 − 2)/0.1 ≈ 0.2485. f(−0.1) = (√3.9 − 2)/(−0.1) ≈ 0.2516. Estimated limit: 0.25. Multiplying by the conjugate gives f(x) = 1/(√(x + 4) + 2) for x ≠ 0. Therefore, lim (x→0) f(x) = 1/(2 + 2) = 1/4. Common slips: rounding the square root too early or losing the negative sign in the denominator at x = −0.1.

Problem 5: (2 + h)³ − 8 = 12h + 6h² + h³. For h ≠ 0, the quotient equals 12 + 6h + h². Therefore, the limit is 12. Common slip: omitting the middle terms in the cube expansion.

Problem 6: For x < 3, |x − 3| = −(x − 3), so the quotient is −1 and the left-hand limit is −1. For x > 3, |x − 3| = x − 3, so the quotient is 1 and the right-hand limit is 1. The two-sided limit does not exist because these limits differ. Common slip: treating the absolute value as x − 3 on both sides.

Problem 7: The left-hand limit is 2c + 1. The right-hand limit is 3. A two-sided limit exists when 2c + 1 = 3, so c = 1. The resulting limit is 3. Look for equality of the one-sided limits. Common slip: using f(1) = 3 alone to conclude that the limit exists.

l_54bcd39f9f2a.summary: Defines continuity at a point and on an interval, classifies discontinuities, and applies the Intermediate Value Theorem; recitation quiz in the problem session.
readings: Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, ch. 2 (to confirm): continuity and the precise definition of a limit

segments.title: Where must the pencil lift?
segments.description:
Say that Weekly online homework: Tangent lines, velocity and the limit of a function is due now. It is submitted online and is each student’s own work.
Put last time’s three functions on the screen again.
Everyone sketches each graph near x = 2 and marks any place the pencil must lift. For each lift, they write a few words naming what fails, the limit or the value at 2.
Hear one student.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: x² − x + 2 has no gap (limit 4, value 4). g has a hole at (2, 4), value undefined. The piecewise f jumps from 3 to 4. Accept informal wording; the precise definition comes next.
shown: Sketch each graph near x = 2. Mark any place where your pencil must lift, and name in a few words what fails.
(c) f(x) = x + 1 for x < 2, and f(x) = x² for x ≥ 2

segments.title: Continuity at a point
segments.description:
State the definition: f is continuous at a when lim (x→a) f(x) = f(a). Unpack it as three requirements: f(a) is defined, the limit exists, and the two are equal.
Revisit the three warm-up functions and last time’s function k, which has limit 4 at 2 but k(2) = 1.
For each one, everyone writes which requirement fails, or that none does, before any answer is given.
Then name each failure aloud as the answers come.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: x² − x + 2 passes all three. g fails the first (undefined at 2). k fails the third (4 ≠ 1). The piecewise f fails the second (one-sided limits 3 and 4). The pencil picture is only a picture; the three requirements are the test.
shown: f is continuous at a when lim (x→a) f(x) = f(a).
1. f(a) is defined.  2. lim (x→a) f(x) exists.  3. The limit equals f(a).
At x = 2, which requirement fails, if any?
(a) x² − x + 2   (b) (x² − 4)/(x − 2)   (c) k, with limit 4 at 2 and k(2) = 1   (d) x + 1 for x < 2, x² for x ≥ 2

segments.title: Testing continuity at a point
segments.description:
Students work four functions alone for six minutes. For each, they compute the limit, find the value, and write continuous or not continuous at the stated point, naming any failed requirement.
Students compare with a neighbor for two minutes.
Go over each, asking for the limit and the value before the verdict.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. f(x) = (x² − x − 6)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 3, f(3) = 5, at 3: limit 5 = f(3), continuous.
2. (x² − 1)/(x² − 3x + 2) at 1: undefined, limit −2, not continuous.
3. x + 1 for x < 2, x² for x ≥ 2, at 2: limits 3 and 4, not continuous.
4. sin x / x for x ≠ 0, f(0) = 1, at 0: limit 1 = f(0), continuous.
Slip: skipping the value f(a).

segments.title: One-sided continuity and continuity on an interval
segments.description:
Define continuous from the right and from the left using the one-sided limits from last time. Define continuous on an interval as continuous at every number in it, with one-sided continuity at a closed endpoint.
Show f(x) = √(4 − x²) on [−2, 2], and the piecewise function from item 3, which is continuous from the right at 2 but not from the left.
State that polynomials, rational functions on their domains, √x, sin x and cos x are continuous there, and that sums, products, quotients and composites keep continuity.
Everyone writes the intervals on which 1/(x − 2) is continuous before it is announced.
segments.teacherNotes: For √(4 − x²) at 2, the left limit is 0 = f(2). Answer for 1/(x − 2): (−∞, 2) and (2, ∞). The number 2 is outside the domain, so say ‘continuous on its domain’ rather than ‘discontinuous function’. Stewart, chapter 2, states these results as theorems.
shown: Continuous from the right at a: lim (x→a⁺) f(x) = f(a). Continuous from the left at a: lim (x→a⁻) f(x) = f(a).
Continuous on an interval: continuous at every number in it, with one-sided continuity at a closed endpoint.
Write the intervals on which r(x) = 1/(x − 2) is continuous.

segments.title: Find the mistake
segments.description:
Students receive three flawed claims. For each, they name the error and write a correct statement.
They work alone for six minutes, then compare with a partner.
Go over each, naming the requirement or definition that was misused.
segments.teacherNotes:
A: the limit is 4, but g(2) is undefined, so g is not continuous at 2.
B: 0 is not in the domain of 1/x. It is continuous on (−∞, 0) and (0, ∞).
C: the left limit 3 is not f(2) = 4. f is continuous from the right at 2 only.
Watch for ‘limit exists, so continuous’.

segments.title: The three requirements
segments.description:
Everyone writes the three requirements for continuity at a from memory, then checks them against a partner’s.
Hear one student state them aloud.
Preview that the next lecture sorts the ways a function can fail to be continuous and uses continuity to find unknown constants.
segments.teacherNotes: Common gap: dropping ‘the limit exists’ as a separate requirement. Ask which requirement fails for g and which for the jump function, to prepare classification.

segments.title: Three ways to fail at x = 3
segments.description:
Put three functions on the screen. For each, everyone writes which continuity requirement fails at x = 3.
Hear one answer per function.
segments.teacherNotes: (a) undefined at 3, limit 5, a hole. (b) undefined; left side falls without bound, right side rises without bound. (c) undefined; left limit −1, right limit 1. Bring out what the graph does on each side when the three types are named in the next segment.

segments.title: Removable, jump and infinite discontinuities
segments.description:
Name the three types using the warm-up functions: removable (a), infinite (b), jump (c). Define each by its limits.
Add the greatest integer function ⌊x⌋ at x = 1, and k from last time. Show that a removable one is repaired by redefining the value, and a jump cannot be.
Everyone writes the value that repairs g(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) at 2 and the value that repairs k, then the size of the jump of ⌊x⌋ at 1.
Say that infinite limits get a full treatment later in the course.
segments.teacherNotes: Repairs: both need the value 4. ⌊x⌋ at 1: left limit 0, right limit 1, jump of size 1. Also note sin(π/x) at 0 fits none of the three because of oscillation. Describe infinite limits informally: the values grow without bound.
shown: Removable: lim (x→a) f(x) exists and is finite, but f(a) is undefined or different.
Jump: both one-sided limits exist and are finite, but they differ.
Infinite: at least one one-sided limit is ∞ or −∞.

segments.title: Classify the discontinuity
segments.description:
Students classify each given discontinuity alone for eight minutes, writing the limits that justify the type. One item is continuous.
They compare with a partner for two minutes.
Go over each, asking for the one-sided limits first.
segments.teacherNotes:
1. (x² − x − 6)/(x − 3) at 3: removable, limit 5.
2. |x − 1|/(x − 1) at 1: jump, −1 and 1.
3. 1/(x + 2)² at −2: infinite, both sides +∞.
4. (x² − 1)/(x² − 3x + 2): at 1 removable (limit −2); at 2 infinite.
5. 3x − 1 for x < 1, x + 1 for x ≥ 1, at 1: continuous.

segments.title: Where is a built-up function continuous?
segments.description:
State that if g is continuous at a and f is continuous at g(a), then f∘g is continuous at a.
Apply it to sin(x² + 1), which is continuous everywhere.
Everyone writes where F(x) = 1/(x² − x − 6) and H(x) = √(x² − 4) are continuous before the answers are shown.
segments.teacherNotes: F: x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2), so continuous except at 3 and −2. H: need x² − 4 ≥ 0, so (−∞, −2] and [2, ∞), with one-sided continuity at the endpoints. Common slip: forgetting the root’s domain.
shown: If g is continuous at a and f is continuous at g(a), then f∘g is continuous at a.

segments.title: Find the constant that makes f continuous
segments.description:
Students work two problems turned around: find the constant c that makes the function continuous. They set the one-sided limits equal to the value.
They work alone for six minutes, then compare with a partner.
Each checks the answer by computing both sides with the c found.
segments.teacherNotes:
1. cx² + 2x for x < 2, x³ − cx for x ≥ 2: 4c + 4 = 8 − 2c, so c = 2/3.
2. (x² − 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2, and c at x = 2: c = 4.
Slip: setting the pieces equal for all x instead of at x = 2.
shown: Find the constant c that makes f continuous at x = 2.
1. f(x) = cx² + 2x for x < 2, and f(x) = x³ − cx for x ≥ 2
2. f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2, and f(2) = c

segments.title: Must a continuous graph cross the axis?
segments.description:
Everyone tries to sketch a continuous graph from (0, −1) to (1, 2) that never meets the x-axis.
Then they sketch a graph with a jump from (0, −1) to (1, 2) that never meets it.
Hear one student say what the two sketches show.
segments.teacherNotes: The first attempt fails; the second succeeds, so continuity is the key. This sets up the Intermediate Value Theorem in the next lecture.

segments.title: Finish the sentence
segments.description:
Everyone completes in writing: if f is continuous on [a, b], f(a) < 0 and f(b) > 0, then ...
Pairs compare, and one is heard.
segments.teacherNotes: Target: f has a root in (a, b). Some will write ‘f crosses the axis’; accept it and tighten the wording in the next segment.
shown: If f is continuous on [a, b], f(a) < 0 and f(b) > 0, then ...

segments.title: The Intermediate Value Theorem
segments.description:
State the theorem and draw it: a horizontal line at height N must cut a continuous graph from (a, f(a)) to (b, f(b)).
Show two failures: f(x) = −1 for x < 0 and 1 for x ≥ 0 on [−1, 1], and 1/x on [−1, 1].
Show that 4x³ − 6x² + 3x − 2 = 0 has a root in (1, 2). Everyone computes f(1) and f(2) themselves, then the five steps are written together: define f, say why it is continuous, evaluate the endpoints, place N between them, conclude.
segments.teacherNotes: f(1) = −1 and f(2) = 12, so N = 0 lies between. For both failures N = 0 lies between the endpoint values yet no c exists, so continuity is needed. The IVT gives existence, not the value of c.
shown: Intermediate Value Theorem: suppose f is continuous on [a, b] and N is strictly between f(a) and f(b). Then there is a number c in (a, b) with f(c) = N.
Show that 4x³ − 6x² + 3x − 2 = 0 has a root in (1, 2).
Steps: (1) define f; (2) f is continuous because it is a polynomial; (3) evaluate f(1) and f(2); (4) 0 lies between them; (5) conclude.

segments.title: Show that the equation has a root
segments.description:
Students write a five-step argument for each equation alone for eight minutes, using the interval given.
They compare with a partner for two minutes.
Two students read one argument aloud.
segments.teacherNotes:
(a) cos x = x on (0, 1): f = cos x − x, f(0) = 1, f(1) ≈ −0.46 (radians).
(b) x⁴ + x − 3 = 0 on (1, 2): f(1) = −1, f(2) = 15.
(c) eˣ = 3 − 2x on (0, 1): f = eˣ + 2x − 3, f(0) = −2, f(1) = e − 1 ≈ 1.72.
Check calculator mode and the continuity step.

segments.title: Trapping the root by halving
segments.description:
Return to 4x³ − 6x² + 3x − 2 on [1, 2]. Everyone predicts the sign of f(1.5), then computes it.
Use the sign to choose the half-interval that holds the root.
Give f(1.25) and f(1.125) on the screen, and students choose the half-interval each time.
Say that each step applies the theorem to a smaller interval.
segments.teacherNotes: f(1.5) = 2.5 > 0, so the root is in (1, 1.5). Given values: f(1.25) = 0.1875 > 0, so it is in (1, 1.25). f(1.125) ≈ −0.523 < 0, so it is in (1.125, 1.25). The root is near 1.2.
shown: Predict the sign of f(1.5), then compute it.
f(1.25) = 0.1875.  f(1.125) ≈ −0.523.  Which half-interval holds the root each time?

segments.title: Find the mistake in each use of the theorem
segments.description:
Students receive three flawed arguments. For each, they name the error and write a correct statement.
They work alone for six minutes, then compare with a partner.
Go over each, naming the hypothesis that was ignored.
segments.teacherNotes:
A: 1/x is not continuous on [−1, 1], and has no root.
B: same-sign endpoint values prove nothing; x² − 4x + 3 has roots 1 and 3.
C: 0 is not between f(0) = 1 and f(2) = 5, and x² + 1 has no root.

segments.title: Continuity and the precise definition of a limit
segments.description:
Link to the reading: for every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 such that 0 < |x − a| < δ implies |f(x) − L| < ε.
Students find a δ for f(x) = 2x + 1 with a = 3, L = 7 and ε = 0.1, then for ε = 0.01.
Read continuity as the same statement with L = f(a), where |x − a| = 0 is allowed.
segments.teacherNotes: |2x + 1 − 7| = 2|x − 3| < 0.1 when |x − 3| < 0.05; for 0.01, δ = 0.005. In general δ = ε/2 works. Any smaller positive δ also works; ask for one that is small enough to guarantee the required bound.
shown: f(x) = 2x + 1, a = 3, L = 7. Find δ so that 0 < |x − 3| < δ guarantees |f(x) − 7| < 0.1.

segments.title: What the problem session holds
segments.description:
Recap the three tools: check three requirements, classify by one-sided limits, and use the IVT with continuity on a closed interval.
Tell students the problem session works problems on all three lectures, then holds the weekly recitation quiz.

keyIdeas: A function f is continuous at a when lim (x→a) f(x) = f(a). This needs three things: f(a) is defined, the limit exists, and the two are equal.

Polynomials, rational functions on their domains, roots, sine and cosine are continuous. Sums, products, quotients (with nonzero denominator) and composites of continuous functions are continuous, so direct substitution is justified for them.
A discontinuity is removable if the limit exists but f(a) is missing or different, a jump if the one-sided limits exist but differ, and infinite if a one-sided limit is ∞ or −∞.
Intermediate Value Theorem: if f is continuous on [a, b] and N lies strictly between f(a) and f(b), then f(c) = N for some c in (a, b). Continuity on the whole closed interval is essential.
The IVT guarantees that a root exists but does not find it. Checking the sign of f at endpoints and midpoints traps the root in smaller and smaller intervals.

vocabulary.definition: f is continuous at a when f(a) is defined, lim (x→a) f(x) exists and lim (x→a) f(x) = f(a).
Continuous at every number in the interval, with one-sided continuity at any closed endpoint.
A number a at which f fails to be continuous.
The limit at a exists and is finite, but f(a) is undefined or different from it. Redefining f(a) repairs it.
Both one-sided limits at a exist and are finite, but they are not equal.
At least one one-sided limit at a is ∞ or −∞.
If f is continuous on [a, b] and N is strictly between f(a) and f(b), then f(c) = N for some c in (a, b).
A number c with f(c) = 0, a solution of the equation f(x) = 0.

study.overview: Continuity says that a function has no break at a point: its graph there can be drawn without lifting the pencil, and the limit and the value agree. This guide covers four ideas. The first is the three-requirement test for continuity at a point. The second is where familiar functions are continuous. The third is the sorting of discontinuities into removable, jump and infinite. The fourth is the Intermediate Value Theorem, which uses continuity on a closed interval to guarantee a root. For the formal statements and proofs, see Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, chapter 2 (to confirm).

points.heading: Continuity at a point is a three-part test
points.explanation:
A function f is continuous at a when lim (x→a) f(x) = f(a). Check three things in order. (1) f(a) is defined. (2) lim (x→a) f(x) exists. (3) The limit equals f(a). The pencil picture is only a picture. The test is the three requirements, and a common slip is to check the limit and forget the value.

Example. Take g(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) at a = 2. For x ≠ 2, g(x) = x + 2, so the limit is 4. But g(2) is undefined, so requirement 1 fails. Now take a function k with limit 4 at 2 and k(2) = 1. Requirements 1 and 2 hold, but 4 ≠ 1, so requirement 3 fails. Finally take f(x) = x + 1 for x < 2 and f(x) = x² for x ≥ 2. The left limit at 2 is 3 and the right limit is 4. The two-sided limit does not exist, so requirement 2 fails. By contrast, x² − x + 2 passes all three at 2: the limit is 4 and the value is 4.

points.heading: Where functions are continuous: one-sided continuity, intervals and building blocks
points.explanation:
Continuous from the right at a means lim (x→a⁺) f(x) = f(a). Continuous from the left means lim (x→a⁻) f(x) = f(a). A function is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every number in it, with one-sided continuity at any closed endpoint. The piecewise function above (x + 1 for x < 2, x² for x ≥ 2) is continuous from the right at 2 because the right limit 4 equals f(2) = 4. It is not continuous from the left, because the left limit is 3.

Polynomials, rational functions on their domains, roots, sin x and cos x are continuous. Sums, products, quotients (with nonzero denominator) and composites of continuous functions are continuous. This is why direct substitution works for them. In particular, if g is continuous at a and f is continuous at g(a), then f∘g is continuous at a.

Example. Let F(x) = 1/(x² − x − 6). Since x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2), F is continuous everywhere except at 3 and −2. Now let H(x) = √(x² − 4). It needs x² − 4 ≥ 0, so H is continuous on (−∞, −2] and [2, ∞), with one-sided continuity at the endpoints. For r(x) = 1/(x − 2), the number 2 is not in the domain. Say that r is continuous on (−∞, 2) and (2, ∞), rather than calling it a discontinuous function.

points.heading: Classifying discontinuities: removable, jump, infinite
points.explanation:
Classify a discontinuity by the one-sided limits. It is removable if lim (x→a) f(x) exists and is finite, but f(a) is undefined or different. It is a jump if both one-sided limits exist and are finite but differ. It is infinite if at least one one-sided limit is ∞ or −∞. A removable discontinuity can be repaired by redefining the value at a. A jump or infinite discontinuity cannot be repaired this way. Some functions fit none of the three. For example, sin(π/x) at 0 oscillates instead.

Example. For g(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2), the limit at 2 is 4 and g(2) is undefined. This is removable, and defining g(2) = 4 repairs it. For the greatest integer function ⌊x⌋ at x = 1, the left limit is 0 and the right limit is 1. This is a jump of size 1, and no choice of ⌊1⌋ closes the gap. For 1/(x − 3) at 3, the values fall without bound on the left and rise without bound on the right. This is an infinite discontinuity. Always write both one-sided limits before naming the type.

points.heading: The Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a root but does not find it
points.explanation:
Intermediate Value Theorem: if f is continuous on [a, b] and N lies strictly between f(a) and f(b), then f(c) = N for some c in (a, b). To show that an equation has a root, use N = 0 and write five steps: (1) define f; (2) say why f is continuous; (3) evaluate f at both endpoints; (4) show that 0 lies between the two values; (5) conclude.

Example. Show that 4x³ − 6x² + 3x − 2 = 0 has a root in (1, 2). Let f(x) = 4x³ − 6x² + 3x − 2. It is a polynomial, so it is continuous on [1, 2]. Then f(1) = −1 and f(2) = 12. Since 0 lies between −1 and 12, there is a c in (1, 2) with f(c) = 0.

Continuity on the whole closed interval is essential. For f(x) = 1/x on [−1, 1], f(−1) = −1 and f(1) = 1, so 0 lies between them. Yet 1/x = 0 has no solution, because f is not continuous at 0. Also, endpoint values of the same sign prove nothing about whether a root exists.

The theorem gives existence, not the value of c. To trap the root, test midpoints. Here f(1.5) = 2.5 > 0, so the root is in (1, 1.5). Next f(1.25) = 0.1875 > 0, so it is in (1, 1.25). Then f(1.125) ≈ −0.523 < 0, so it is in (1.125, 1.25). Each step applies the theorem to a smaller interval, and the root is near 1.2.

handouts.title: Testing continuity at a point

blocks.text: Work alone. For each function, compute the limit at the stated point, find the value of the function there, and write continuous or not continuous. If it is not continuous, name the requirement that fails.
1. f(x) = (x² − x − 6)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 3, and f(3) = 5. Point: x = 3.
3. f(x) = x + 1 for x < 2, and f(x) = x² for x ≥ 2. Point: x = 2.
4. f(x) = sin x / x for x ≠ 0, and f(0) = 1. Point: x = 0.

handouts.key:
1. For x ≠ 3, x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2), so f(x) = x + 2. Limit: lim (x→3) f(x) = 5. Value: f(3) = 5. Verdict: continuous at 3; all three requirements hold.

2. For x ≠ 1, 2, f(x) = (x − 1)(x + 1)/[(x − 1)(x − 2)] = (x + 1)/(x − 2). Limit: lim (x→1) f(x) = 2/(−1) = −2. Value: f(1) is undefined. Verdict: not continuous at 1 because the function value is undefined. Common slip: cancellation does not define the original function at 1.

3. Left-hand limit: lim (x→2⁻) f(x) = 3. Right-hand limit: lim (x→2⁺) f(x) = 4. Limit: the two-sided limit does not exist. Value: f(2) = 4. Verdict: not continuous at 2 because the two-sided limit does not exist. Common slip: using only the branch that gives f(2).

4. Limit: lim (x→0) sin x / x = 1, with x measured in radians. Value: f(0) = 1. Verdict: continuous at 0; all three requirements hold. Common slip: direct substitution gives an undefined quotient, not the limit.

handouts.title: Find the mistake: continuity

blocks.text: Each claim below contains an error. Name the error, then write a correct statement.
Claim A. Let g(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2). Since the limit of g(x) as x → 2 is 4, g is continuous at 2.

blocks.hint: The error, and a correct statement.

blocks.text: Claim B. The function f(x) = 1/x is a rational function, so it is continuous on (−∞, ∞).

blocks.hint: The error, and a correct statement.

blocks.text: Claim C. Let f(x) = x + 1 for x < 2 and f(x) = x² for x ≥ 2, so f(2) = 4. The left-hand limit of f at 2 exists and equals 3, so f is continuous from the left at 2.

blocks.hint: The error, and a correct statement.

handouts.key:
Claim A. Error: existence of the limit does not establish continuity when g(2) is undefined. For x ≠ 2, g(x) = x + 2, so lim (x→2) g(x) = 4. Correct statement: g is not continuous at 2 because g(2) is undefined; defining g(2) = 4 would make the extended function continuous there. Look for an explicit distinction between the limit and the function value.

Claim B. Error: a rational function is continuous only where its denominator is nonzero. Correct statement: 1/x is continuous on (−∞, 0) and (0, ∞); it is undefined at 0. Common slip: treating a continuity theorem as if it removed domain restrictions.

Claim C. Error: left continuity requires the left-hand limit to equal f(2), not merely to exist. Here lim (x→2⁻) f(x) = 3 ≠ 4 = f(2). Correct statement: f is not continuous from the left at 2. It is continuous from the right because lim (x→2⁺) f(x) = 4 = f(2). Look for both the limit and the value in the comparison.

handouts.title: Classify the discontinuity

blocks.text: For each function at the stated point, write the one-sided limits and decide: removable, jump, infinite, or continuous. One item is continuous, and one item has two points to check.
4. f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x² − 3x + 2) at x = 1 and at x = 2.

blocks.hint: At each point: left limit, right limit, type.

blocks.text: 5. f(x) = 3x − 1 for x < 1, and f(x) = x + 1 for x ≥ 1, at x = 1.

blocks.hint: Left limit, right limit, value, type.

handouts.key:
1. For x ≠ 3, f(x) = x + 2. Left limit: 5. Right limit: 5. Type: removable discontinuity, since f(3) is undefined but the finite two-sided limit exists. The repairing value is f(3) = 5.

2. For x < 1, |x − 1|/(x − 1) = −1; for x > 1, it equals 1. Left limit: −1. Right limit: 1. Type: jump discontinuity. Common slip: assuming the absolute value makes the quotient positive on both sides.

3. As x approaches −2 from either side, (x + 2)² approaches 0 through positive values. Left limit: +∞. Right limit: +∞. Type: infinite discontinuity. Common slip: assigning a negative sign to the left-hand limit despite the squared denominator.

4. For x ≠ 1, 2, f(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 2).
At x = 1: left limit −2; right limit −2; type removable, since f(1) is undefined. Defining f(1) = −2 repairs it.
At x = 2: left limit −∞; right limit +∞; type infinite. The numerator approaches 3, while the denominator approaches 0 from opposite sides. Common slip: canceling x − 1 and overlooking the remaining denominator x − 2.

5. Left limit: 3(1) − 1 = 2. Right limit: 1 + 1 = 2. Value: f(1) = 2. Type: continuous at 1. Look for agreement of both one-sided limits with the function value.

blocks.text: For each equation, write a complete argument using the Intermediate Value Theorem on the interval given. Your argument has five steps: define f, say why f is continuous, evaluate f at the endpoints, place N = 0 between the two values, and conclude. Use radians for cos x.
(a) cos x = x on the interval (0, 1).
(b) x⁴ + x − 3 = 0 on the interval (1, 2).
(c) eˣ = 3 − 2x on the interval (0, 1).

handouts.key:
(a) Define f(x) = cos x − x. It is continuous on [0, 1] because cosine and the identity function are continuous. Using radians, f(0) = 1 and f(1) = cos 1 − 1 ≈ −0.4597. Thus f(1) < 0 < f(0). By the Intermediate Value Theorem, there is a c ∈ (0, 1) with f(c) = 0, so cos c = c.

(b) Define f(x) = x⁴ + x − 3. As a polynomial, f is continuous on [1, 2]. Its endpoint values are f(1) = 1 + 1 − 3 = −1 and f(2) = 16 + 2 − 3 = 15. Thus f(1) < 0 < f(2). By the Intermediate Value Theorem, there is a c ∈ (1, 2) with f(c) = 0, so c⁴ + c − 3 = 0.

(c) Define f(x) = eˣ + 2x − 3. It is continuous on [0, 1] because exponential and polynomial functions are continuous. Its endpoint values are f(0) = 1 − 3 = −2 and f(1) = e + 2 − 3 = e − 1 ≈ 1.7183. Thus f(0) < 0 < f(1). By the Intermediate Value Theorem, there is a c ∈ (0, 1) with f(c) = 0, so eᶜ = 3 − 2c.

Look for all five steps in each argument, including continuity on the closed interval and a conclusion in the open interval. Common slips: omitting continuity, using degrees for cosine, or claiming the theorem gives an exact root or a unique root.

handouts.title: Find the mistake in each use of the theorem
handouts.usedIn: Find the mistake in each use of the theorem

blocks.text: Each argument below misuses the Intermediate Value Theorem. Name the error, then write a correct statement.
Argument A. Let f(x) = 1/x on [−1, 1]. Then f(−1) = −1 and f(1) = 1, and 0 lies between them. By the Intermediate Value Theorem, 1/x = 0 has a solution in (−1, 1).

blocks.hint: The error, and a correct statement.

blocks.text: Argument B. Let f(x) = x² − 4x + 3 on [0, 4]. Then f(0) = 3 and f(4) = 3, both positive. By the Intermediate Value Theorem, f has no root in (0, 4).

blocks.hint: The error, and a correct statement.

blocks.text: Argument C. Let f(x) = x² + 1, which is continuous. Then f(0) = 1 and f(2) = 5. By the Intermediate Value Theorem, f has a root in (0, 2).

blocks.hint: The error, and a correct statement.

handouts.key:
Argument A. Error: 1/x is undefined at 0 and therefore is not continuous on [−1, 1]. Correct statement: the Intermediate Value Theorem does not apply on this interval. The equation 1/x = 0 has no solution because a reciprocal with numerator 1 is never zero. Look for both the failed hypothesis and a separate reason for the absence of a root.

Argument B. Error: positive endpoint values do not imply that a continuous function has no root between them. Correct statement: f(x) = x² − 4x + 3 = (x − 1)(x − 3) has roots at x = 1 and x = 3, both in (0, 4). The endpoint values f(0) = f(4) = 3 do not establish the absence of roots. Common slip: treating opposite endpoint signs as necessary for roots to exist.

Argument C. Error: 0 is not between f(0) = 1 and f(2) = 5. Correct statement: the Intermediate Value Theorem does not guarantee a root from these endpoint values. In fact, x² + 1 ≥ 1 for every real x, so f has no real root. Look for the missing target-value condition and the positivity argument.

handouts.title: Problems on continuity and the IVT
handouts.usedIn: Problems on continuity and the IVT

blocks.text: Work in pairs. Try each problem before any solution is shown. Name the definition or theorem you use at each step.
1. Let f(x) = (x² − 16)/(x − 4) for x ≠ 4, and f(4) = 7. Is f continuous at 4? If not, what value of f(4) would make it continuous?
2. Find and classify every discontinuity of f(x) = (x² − x − 2)/(x² − 4). Give the limits that justify each type.
3. Find the constant c that makes f continuous at 3, where f(x) = cx + 1 for x ≤ 3 and f(x) = cx² − 1 for x > 3.
4. Write the intervals on which f(x) = √(x − 1)/(x − 5) is continuous.
5. Use the Intermediate Value Theorem to show that x³ − 3x + 1 = 0 has at least three real roots. Give an interval for each root and the endpoint values you use.
6. A student argues: for f(x) = 1/(x − 1) on [0, 2], f(0) = −1 and f(2) = 1, so by the Intermediate Value Theorem f has a root in (0, 2). Is the argument valid? Does f have a root in (0, 2)? Explain.

handouts.key:
1. For x ≠ 4, f(x) = (x − 4)(x + 4)/(x − 4) = x + 4. Therefore lim (x→4) f(x) = 8, whereas f(4) = 7. By the definition of continuity, f is not continuous at 4. Defining f(4) = 8 makes it continuous there. Common slip: using the simplified formula to replace the stated value 7 without acknowledging the distinction.

2. Factor and cancel for x ≠ −2, 2: f(x) = (x − 2)(x + 1)/[(x − 2)(x + 2)] = (x + 1)/(x + 2). The original function is undefined at −2 and 2 and continuous elsewhere by continuity of rational functions on their domains.
At x = 2: both one-sided limits equal 3/4. This is a removable discontinuity.
At x = −2: lim (x→−2⁻) f(x) = +∞ and lim (x→−2⁺) f(x) = −∞. This is an infinite discontinuity. Near −2, the numerator is negative; the denominator is negative on the left and positive on the right. Common slips: forgetting the original exclusion at 2 or reversing the infinite-limit signs.

3. The left-hand limit and value at 3 are both 3c + 1. The right-hand limit is 9c − 1. Continuity requires 3c + 1 = 9c − 1, giving 6c = 2 and c = 1/3. With this value, the left limit, right limit, and f(3) all equal 2. Look for equality at the joining point, rather than equality of the two formulas for every x.

4. The square root requires x ≥ 1, and the denominator requires x ≠ 5. By the continuity rules for square roots and quotients, f is continuous on [1, 5) and (5, ∞). At 1, the right-hand limit equals f(1) = 0, so the closed endpoint is included. Common slips: omitting 1 or including 5.

5. Define f(x) = x³ − 3x + 1. This polynomial is continuous on every closed interval used below.
On [−2, −1], f(−2) = −8 + 6 + 1 = −1 and f(−1) = −1 + 3 + 1 = 3. The Intermediate Value Theorem gives a root in (−2, −1).
On [0, 1], f(0) = 1 and f(1) = 1 − 3 + 1 = −1. The Intermediate Value Theorem gives a root in (0, 1).
On [1, 2], f(1) = −1 and f(2) = 8 − 6 + 1 = 3. The Intermediate Value Theorem gives a root in (1, 2).
The open intervals are disjoint, so these are at least three distinct real roots. Look for continuity, opposite endpoint signs for each interval, and an explanation of distinctness. Common slip: listing sign changes without identifying the intervals they establish.

6. The argument is invalid. Although f(0) = −1 and f(2) = 1, f is undefined at 1 and is not continuous on [0, 2]. The Intermediate Value Theorem therefore does not apply. The function has no root in (0, 2): wherever it is defined, its numerator is 1, so 1/(x − 1) cannot equal 0. Look for separate answers about the argument's validity and the actual existence of a root. Common slip: concluding that failure of the continuity hypothesis alone proves there is no root.

t_3189cd32a2e7.prompt: What is the same in the tangent problem and the velocity problem? In the first, the slope of the tangent to y = x² at P(1, 1) came from secant slopes (x² − 1)/(x − 1) that got close to 2. In the second, a ball falling s(t) = 4.9t² meters had average velocities of 49.49, 49.049 and 49.0049 m/s on [5, 5.1], [5, 5.01] and [5, 5.001], which got close to 49 m/s. Compare how each number was built and what happened to the interval.
followUps: What would happen to each ratio if we set the width of the interval to 0 right away, and why can we not simply do that?
The three secant slopes 2.1, 2.01 and 1.99 suggest 2, and so does the simplification to x + 1. Which do you trust more, and why?
Could a quantity that has nothing to do with motion or geometry, such as a rate of change in a population, lead to the same structure? What would the ratio be?

t_2a2b0bf6392a.prompt: At x = 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 and 1/5, the values of sin(π/x) are all 0, so a table suggests the limit as x → 0 is 0. At x = 2/5, 2/9 and 2/13, the value is 1. What do the two tables together say about relying on a table alone to find a limit?
followUps: Why did the first table seem convincing, and what did we assume about the x-values we chose?
The table for sin x / x gave 0.9583 and 0.9983 and we estimated 1. What makes us more willing to believe that estimate, and what would we want to back it up?
Does a table ever count as proof of a limit? If not, what does it give us, and what would you add to turn it into an argument?

t_426e1c42a412.explanation: The table values approach 7 from both sides of 3. “−2” uses r(3) instead of nearby values. “3” confuses the input approached with the output approached. “The limit does not exist” incorrectly treats a different value at x = 3 as preventing a limit. The table supports an estimate, not a proof.

t_94b8f2d1edfc.prompt: The graph of v has a horizontal branch at height 2 for x < −1 and a horizontal branch at height −3 for x > −1. Both branches have open endpoints at x = −1. A filled point is at (−1, 4). What is lim (x→−1) v(x)?
t_94b8f2d1edfc.explanation: The left-hand limit is 2 and the right-hand limit is −3. Since they differ, “No limit exists” is correct. “The limit is 2” uses only the left-hand limit. “The limit is −3” uses only the right-hand limit. “The limit is 4” uses the filled point, which gives v(−1).

t_bc9ed20dc1b3.explanation: Factor x² + x − 12 as (x − 3)(x + 4). For x ≠ 3, the quotient equals x + 4, so its limit is 7. “6” results from incorrectly factoring the numerator as (x − 3)(x + 3). “0” treats 0/0 as zero. “The limit does not exist” confuses an undefined function value with a nonexistent limit.

t_3d4514233f20.prompt: For w(x) = x² + 1 when x ≠ −2 and w(−2) = 9, lim (x→−2) w(x) = 5.
t_3d4514233f20.explanation: Near −2, the function follows x² + 1. Direct substitution into that polynomial gives (−2)² + 1 = 5. The assigned value w(−2) = 9 does not change the limit.

t_1a4115fef1be.prompt: A student evaluates lim (u→0) (√(16 + u) − 4)/u. After multiplying by the conjugate, the student writes 1/√(16 + u) and concludes that the limit is 1/4. Identify the mistake and give a correct solution. Explain why canceling u is allowed.
t_1a4115fef1be.answer: The student dropped the +4 from the denominator. Multiplying the numerator and denominator by √(16 + u) + 4 gives u/[u(√(16 + u) + 4)]. For u ≠ 0, this simplifies to 1/(√(16 + u) + 4). Canceling u is allowed because the limit considers u near 0 with u ≠ 0. The limit is 1/(4 + 4) = 1/8.
t_1a4115fef1be.explanation: The conjugate produces (16 + u) − 16 = u in the numerator, while the denominator remains u(√(16 + u) + 4). Canceling the nonzero factor u leaves the entire conjugate in the denominator. Substitution then gives 1/8.

t_fe8431376de9.prompt: Can you sketch a continuous graph from (0, −1) to (1, 2) that never meets the x-axis? Try it. Then sketch a graph with a jump that goes from (0, −1) to (1, 2) and never meets the x-axis. What do the two sketches show about continuity?
followUps: In your continuous attempt, where did the graph have to pass from below the axis to above it, and what did you have to give up to avoid touching the axis?
What exactly does the jump sketch do that the continuous sketch cannot, and which of the three requirements for continuity fails at that point?
If the graph ran from (0, 1) to (1, 2), would it have to cross the x-axis? What does that tell you about the role of the number 0 lying between −1 and 2?

t_948d70649f47.prompt: Take f(x) = 1/x on [−1, 1]. Here f(−1) = −1 and f(1) = 1, so N = 0 lies between the endpoint values. One student says the Intermediate Value Theorem therefore guarantees a root in (−1, 1). But 1/x never equals 0. Is the theorem wrong, or is the student’s argument wrong? Defend your side.

None of the continuity requirements fails.

Since p(5) = 7, the limit does not equal the value. “The value p(5) is defined.” overlooks the assigned value 7. “The limit as x → 5 exists.” mistakes the original denominator being zero for a nonexistent limit. “None of the continuity requirements fails.” ignores that 10 ≠ 7.

t_47dd84259905.prompt: Let q(x) = x + 2 for x < 1, and q(x) = 2x + 3 for x ≥ 1. How is q classified at x = 1?

choices.text: It is continuous at the point.

t_47dd84259905.explanation: The left-hand limit is 3 and the right-hand limit is 5. These finite limits differ, so q has a jump discontinuity. “It has a removable discontinuity.” would require a finite two-sided limit. “It has an infinite discontinuity.” would require values growing without bound on at least one side. “It is continuous at the point.” checks neither the mismatch between the one-sided limits nor the missing two-sided limit.

t_b167754ff948.prompt: Let r(x) = x³ + x − 5. Which interval has endpoint values with opposite signs, allowing the Intermediate Value Theorem to guarantee a root inside it?
t_b167754ff948.explanation: The polynomial r is continuous on every closed interval. Since r(1) = −3 and r(2) = 5, the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a root in (1, 2). “(0, 1)” has endpoint values −5 and −3, both negative. “(2, 3)” has endpoint values 5 and 25, both positive. “(3, 4)” has endpoint values 25 and 63, both positive.

t_b96be7dcd706.prompt: Let s(x) = 2 for x < 0 and s(x) = 4 for x > 0. Defining s(0) = 3 makes s continuous at 0.
t_b96be7dcd706.explanation: The left-hand limit is 2 and the right-hand limit is 4. The two-sided limit does not exist. Choosing a value at 0 cannot repair this jump.

t_8d47b65fac20.prompt: A student argues: “For h(x) = x² − 6x + 8, h(0) = 8 and h(5) = 3. Both endpoint values are positive, so the Intermediate Value Theorem proves there is no root in (0, 5).” Identify the mistake. Then use the Intermediate Value Theorem on smaller intervals to prove that h has at least two distinct roots in (0, 5).
t_8d47b65fac20.answer: Same-sign endpoint values do not prove that there is no root. The polynomial h is continuous on [0, 3] and [3, 5]. Since h(0) = 8, h(3) = −1 and h(5) = 3, the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a root in (0, 3) and a root in (3, 5). These intervals are disjoint, so the roots are distinct.
t_8d47b65fac20.explanation: The Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a root when 0 lies between the endpoint values of a continuous function. It does not rule out roots when the endpoint values have the same sign. Evaluating h(3) = 9 − 18 + 8 = −1 provides a negative value between the positive endpoint values. Applying the theorem separately to [0, 3] and [3, 5] establishes two distinct roots.

Show algebraic steps and give reasons where requested. Weekly recitation quizzes are marked in points and count equally within the component, which is worth 15% of the course grade.
steps:
The table shows values of a function F near x = −1.

x | F(x)
−1.1 | 3.210000
−1.01 | 3.020100
−1.001 | 3.002001
−0.999 | 2.998001
−0.99 | 2.980100

Also, F(−1) = 8.
(a) Estimate lim (x→−1) F(x).
(b) Explain how the values on both sides support your estimate and why F(−1) does not change it. (3 points)

The graph of G consists of two straight rays and one filled point. The left ray passes through (−1, 1) and (0, 2) and ends at an open point at (1, 3). The right ray starts at an open point at (1, 5) and passes through (2, 3) and (3, 1). A filled point is at (1, 0).
(a) Find lim (x→1⁻) G(x).
(b) Find lim (x→1⁺) G(x).
(c) Does lim (x→1) G(x) exist? Explain using your one-sided limits. (4 points)
Evaluate lim (x→−1) (2x² − 3x + 4)/(x + 5). Show your substitution and explain why the quotient law applies. (3 points)

Evaluate each limit. Show the rewriting and cancellation before substituting.
(a) lim (x→−3) (x² + 5x + 6)/(x + 3)
(b) lim (x→5) (√(x + 20) − 5)/(x − 5) (6 points)
t_5c1bd7cc9ef6.answerKey:
1. (a) The estimated limit is 3: 1 point.
(b) As x approaches −1 from the left, the table values approach 3 from above; from the right, they approach 3 from below: 1 point for using both sides. The limit concerns values near −1 with x ≠ −1, so the value F(−1) = 8 does not change the estimate: 1 point. (3 points)
2. (a) The left-hand limit is 3: 1 point.
(b) The right-hand limit is 5: 1 point.
(c) The two-sided limit does not exist: 1 point. The one-sided limits differ, since 3 ≠ 5: 1 point. The filled point gives G(1) = 0 but does not determine the limit. (4 points)
3. The numerator approaches 2(−1)² − 3(−1) + 4 = 9: 1 point. The denominator approaches −1 + 5 = 4 ≠ 0, so the quotient law applies: 1 point. The limit is 9/4: 1 point. (3 points)
4. (a) Factor x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3): 1 point. For x ≠ −3, cancel x + 3 to obtain x + 2: 1 point. Substitute −3 to obtain the limit −1: 1 point.
(b) Multiply numerator and denominator by √(x + 20) + 5. The numerator becomes (x + 20) − 25 = x − 5: 1 point. For x ≠ 5, cancel x − 5 to obtain 1/(√(x + 20) + 5): 1 point. Substitute 5 to obtain 1/(5 + 5) = 1/10: 1 point. (6 points)

t_0c204761bb99.prompt: Complete this assignment individually. Show your calculations and explain your conclusions in complete sentences where requested. steps: A table gives A(3.9) = 10.01, A(3.99) = 10.0001, A(3.999) = 10.000001, A(4.001) = 10.000001, A(4.01) = 10.0001 and A(4.1) = 10.01. Also, A(4) = −5. Estimate lim (x→4) A(x). Explain how values from both sides support your estimate, why A(4) does not determine the limit, and why the table alone does not prove your estimate.

Sketch the graph of B, where B(x) = 2x + 10 for x < −3, B(−3) = 0, and B(x) = x² − 2 for x > −3. Mark open endpoints and the filled point. Find lim (x→−3⁻) B(x) and lim (x→−3⁺) B(x). Decide whether lim (x→−3) B(x) exists, and explain your conclusion using the one-sided limits.

Evaluate both limits and show your reasoning: (a) lim (x→2) (3x² − x + 5)/(x + 4); (b) lim (x→4) (x² − 7x + 12)/(x − 4). For (a), explain why the quotient law applies. For (b), show the factorization and state the restriction under which cancellation is valid. Explain why direct substitution works in (a) but requires rewriting in (b).

Evaluate lim (z→0) (√(25 + 2z) − 5)/z. Show the conjugate multiplication, simplification and substitution. Explain why canceling z is legitimate even though the original expression is undefined at z = 0.

On the curve y = x³, let P(2, 8) and Q(2 + h, (2 + h)³) be distinct points. Use m_PQ = ((2 + h)³ − 8)/h, with h ≠ 0. Expand and simplify this secant slope. Compute it for h = 0.1 and h = −0.1. Then use its limit as h → 0 to find the tangent slope at P and write the tangent line in the form y = mx + b. Explain how the secant calculations support your result.

Suppose a cart moves along a straight track with position d(t) = 3t² + 2t feet, where t is measured in seconds. For h > 0, its average velocity over [3, 3 + h] is (d(3 + h) − d(3))/h. Expand and simplify this expression. Compute the average velocities for h = 0.2 and h = 0.02, then take the limit as h → 0⁺ to find the instantaneous velocity at t = 3. Include units and explain what the limit describes.
t_0c204761bb99.answerKey:
1. The estimate is lim (x→4) A(x) = 10. Values on both sides approach 10 as x approaches 4. A(4) = −5 does not affect behavior near 4 with x ≠ 4. The table samples only finitely many inputs; other nearby inputs could behave differently, so it supports an estimate rather than proving the limit.
2. The left line has an open endpoint at (−3, 4). The right parabola has an open endpoint at (−3, 7). The filled point is (−3, 0). The left-hand limit is 2(−3) + 10 = 4. The right-hand limit is (−3)² − 2 = 7. Since 4 ≠ 7, the two-sided limit does not exist.
3. (a) Substitution gives (3·2² − 2 + 5)/(2 + 4) = 15/6 = 5/2. The numerator and denominator have limits, and the denominator’s limit is 6 ≠ 0, so the quotient law applies. (b) x² − 7x + 12 = (x − 3)(x − 4). For x ≠ 4, the quotient equals x − 3, whose limit at 4 is 1. Substitution in the original expression gives 0/0, so rewriting is needed before substitution.
4. Multiply numerator and denominator by √(25 + 2z) + 5. The result is 2z/[z(√(25 + 2z) + 5)] = 2/(√(25 + 2z) + 5) for z ≠ 0. The limit is 2/(5 + 5) = 1/5. Cancellation is valid at nearby nonzero inputs, which are the inputs used to determine the limit.
5. (2 + h)³ = 8 + 12h + 6h² + h³, so m_PQ = 12 + 6h + h² for h ≠ 0. At h = 0.1, the slope is 12.61; at h = −0.1, it is 11.41. The limit is 12. Thus y − 8 = 12(x − 2), or y = 12x − 16. The sampled slopes approach 12 from opposite sides, consistent with the simplified expression’s limit.
6. d(3) = 33 feet and d(3 + h) = 33 + 20h + 3h² feet. The average velocity is (20h + 3h²)/h = 20 + 3h feet per second. At h = 0.2 it is 20.6 ft/s; at h = 0.02 it is 20.06 ft/s. The limit as h → 0⁺ is 20 ft/s. This is the cart’s instantaneous velocity at t = 3, obtained as the limit of average velocities over shrinking intervals.

t_7174431ad249.title: Weekly recitation quizzes: Continuity and the Intermediate Value Theorem
t_7174431ad249.prompt: Time allowed: 18 minutes. The teacher will announce the quiz conditions. Show the calculations and reasoning requested. Use one-sided limits to justify discontinuity classifications. For an Intermediate Value Theorem argument, state why the function is continuous, evaluate the endpoints, and explain the conclusion. This paper is marked in points and counts equally with the other papers in Weekly recitation quizzes (15% of the course grade).
steps: Let u(x) = (x² + x − 12)/(x + 4) for x ≠ −4, and let u(−4) = −7. Compute lim (x→−4) u(x), state u(−4), and decide whether u is continuous at −4. Justify your decision using the requirements for continuity. (3 points)

For each function, find both one-sided limits at the stated point and classify the discontinuity as removable, jump, or infinite.
(a) v(x) = 2x − 1 for x < −1, and v(x) = x + 4 for x ≥ −1. Point: x = −1.
(b) w(x) = 1/(x − 4)². Point: x = 4. (6 points)

Let z(x) = cx + 2 for x < −2, and z(x) = x² + c for x ≥ −2. Find the constant c that makes z continuous at −2. Show the equation you solve, then verify that both one-sided limits equal z(−2). (4 points)

Use the Intermediate Value Theorem to show that x³ − x − 1 = 0 has a root in (1, 2). Define a suitable function, justify its continuity on the closed interval, calculate its endpoint values, and state precisely what the theorem guarantees. (5 points)
t_7174431ad249.answerKey:
1. For x ≠ −4, u(x) = (x + 4)(x − 3)/(x + 4) = x − 3, so lim (x→−4) u(x) = −7. Award 1 point for the correct limit with the factoring and cancellation. The value u(−4) = −7; award 1 point. The value is defined, the limit exists, and the limit equals the value, so u is continuous at −4; award 1 point for this justified conclusion. (3 points)
2. (a) lim (x→−1⁻) v(x) = 2(−1) − 1 = −3, and lim (x→−1⁺) v(x) = −1 + 4 = 3. Award 1 point for each one-sided limit. The finite one-sided limits differ, so the discontinuity is a jump; award 1 point.
(b) As x approaches 4 from either side, (x − 4)² approaches 0 through positive values. Thus lim (x→4⁻) w(x) = +∞ and lim (x→4⁺) w(x) = +∞. Award 1 point for each one-sided limit. The discontinuity is infinite; award 1 point. (6 points)
3. Continuity requires −2c + 2 = 4 + c; award 1 point for this equation. Solving gives −3c = 2, so c = −2/3; award 1 point. With this value, lim (x→−2⁻) z(x) = −2(−2/3) + 2 = 10/3; award 1 point for this verification. Also, lim (x→−2⁺) z(x) = 4 − 2/3 = 10/3 = z(−2); award 1 point for verifying the right-hand limit and value. (4 points)
4. Define P(x) = x³ − x − 1; award 1 point. P is a polynomial, so it is continuous on [1, 2]; award 1 point. P(1) = 1 − 1 − 1 = −1 and P(2) = 8 − 2 − 1 = 5; award 1 point for each endpoint calculation. Since −1 < 0 < 5, the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees some c in (1, 2) with P(c) = 0. Thus the equation has a root in (1, 2); award 1 point for the comparison and precise conclusion. (5 points)
Total: 18 points
